q-32919.name: Question 1
q-32919.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=t\,i+2\sqrt{t}\,j+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+3}\,k$ at the point $P(1,2,2).$
q-32919.worked_solution:
The point $P(1,2,2)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+2\,j+2\,k \\ t\,i+2\sqrt{t}\,j+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+3}\,k & =i+2\,j+2\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}t=1 \\ 2\sqrt{t}=2 \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+3}=2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,2,2)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$  

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+3})\,k \\  & =\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,j+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+3}}\,k \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1)}}\,j+\frac{(1)}{\sqrt{(1)^{2}+3}}\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a tangent vector to the curve at the point $P(1,2,2)$ is $\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k.$

q-126738.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=(1-t)\,i-{t}^{2}\,j+(2t+1)\,k$ at the point $P(2,-1,-1).$
q-126738.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,-1,-1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i-j-k \\ (1-t)\,i-{t}^{2}\,j+(2t+1)\,k & =2\,i-j-k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1-t=2 \\ -{t}^{2}=-1 \\ 2t+1=-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=-1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,-1,-1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(-1).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,k \\  & =-i-2t\,j+2\,k \\ {r}^{′}(-1) & =-i-2(-1)\,j+2\,k \\  & =-i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,-1,-1)$ is $-i+2\,j+2\,k.$

q-75197.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨t+\frac{1}{t},\,t-\frac{1}{t}⟩$ at the point where $t=1.$
q-75197.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=1$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(1)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1-\frac{1}{{1}^{2}},\,1+\frac{1}{{1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨1-1,\,1+1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=1$  is  $⟨0,\,2⟩.$

q-32872.name: Question 4
q-32872.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=2t\,i+(1+{t}^{2})\,j+{t}^{3}\,k$ at the point $P(2,2,1).$
q-32872.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,2,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$  At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+2\,j+\,k \\ 2t\,i+(1+{t}^{2})\,j+{t}^{3}\,k & =2\,i+2\,j+\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2t=2 \\ 1+{t}^{2}=2 \\ {t}^{3}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,2,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})\,+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,k \\  & =2\,i+2t\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =2\,i+2(1)\,j+3(1)^{2}\,k \\  & =2\,i+2\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,2,1)$ is $2\,i+2\,j+3\,k.$

q-75199.name: Question 5
q-75199.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,{t}^{2}⟩$ at the point where $t=0.$
q-75199.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{-t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t},\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-{e}^{-0},\,2\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is $⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩.$

q-126832.name: Question 6
q-126832.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨t+3,\,1-t,\,{t}^{2}⟩$ at the point $P(4,0,1),$ valid for all real values of $u?$
q-126832.worked_solution:
The point $P(4,0,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨4,0,1⟩ \\ ⟨t+3,1-t,{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨4,0,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the components yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}t+3=4 \\ 1-t=0 \\ {t}^{2}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 
From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other equation. Therefore,  $P(4,0,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,-1,2(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point  $P(4,0,1)$ is

$$

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨t+3,1−t,t2⟩ at the point P(4,0,1), valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨0,−2,1⟩+u⟨4,−1,2⟩
b
 ⟨4,0,1⟩+u⟨−2,2,1⟩
c
⟨1,0,2⟩+u⟨4,−1,2⟩
d
⟨4,0,1⟩+u⟨1,−1,2⟩
e
⟨1,0,2⟩+u⟨1,−1,2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The point P(4,0,1) is at the tip of r(t) for some specific value t0 of the parameter t. At this point, the vector r′(t0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(t0)+ur′(t0),u∈(−∞,∞).

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to P. We know that r(t)=⟨4,0,1⟩⟨t+3,1−t,t2⟩=⟨4,0,1⟩,

and equating the components yields the following system: {t+3=41−t=0t2=1 From the first equation, we get t=1. This value also satisfies the other equation. Therefore, P(4,0,1) is at the tip of the vector r(1).

We calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(t+3),ddt(1−t),ddt(t2)⟩=⟨1,−1,2t⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=1: r′(1)=⟨1,−1,2(1)⟩=⟨1,−1,2⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point P(4,0,1) is
R(u)=⟨4,0,1⟩+u⟨1,−1,2⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

q-33461.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{sin}^{2}t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
q-33461.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{4})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j+{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j-\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})k \\  & =\,i-\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
R(u)=\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k+u(\,i-\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj+sin2tk at the point corresponding to t=π4, valid for all real values of u?

a
i+j+12k+u(−i+2j+k)
b
i+j+12k+u(i−j+k)
c
i+j+12k+u(i−j+12k)
d
i+j+12k+u(i+2j+12k)
e
i+j+12k+u(2i−j+k)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=π4, the vector r′(π4) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(π4)+ur′(π4),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(π4):

r(π4)=2sin⁡(π4)i+2cos⁡(π4)j+sin2(π4)k=i+j+12k

Now, we calculate r′(t):

r′(t)=ddt(2sin⁡t)i+ddt(2cos⁡t)j+ddt(sin2t)k=2cos⁡ti−2sin⁡tj+2sin⁡tcos⁡tk

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=π4:

r′(π4)=2cos⁡(π4)i+2sin⁡(π4)j−2sin⁡(π4)cos⁡(π4)k=i−j+k

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=π4 is
R(u)=i+j+12k+u(i−j+k),u∈(−∞,∞).

q-126841.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1),1-5t⟩$ at the point where $t=0,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
q-126841.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+1),1-5(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-5t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1},-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+1},-5⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$

Question 8

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨ln⁡(t2+1),1−5t⟩ at the point where t=0, valid for all real values of u?

a
 ⟨0,1⟩+u⟨2,0⟩
b
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨2,0⟩
c
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨2,−5⟩
d
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩
e
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=0, the vector r′(0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(0)+ur′(0),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(0): r(0)=⟨ln⁡(02+1),1−5(0)⟩=⟨0,1⟩

Now, we calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(ln⁡(t2+1)),ddt(1−5t)⟩=⟨2tt2+1,−5⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=0: r′(0)=⟨2(0)02+1,−5⟩=⟨0,−5⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=0 is
R(u)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

q-32917.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t}-1\,,{e}^{-2t}\,⟩$ at the point $P(0,1),$ valid for all real values of $u?$
q-32917.worked_solution:
The point $P(0,1)$  is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t}-1\,,{e}^{-2t}⟩ & =⟨0,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the components yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}-1=0 \\ {e}^{-2t}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other equation. Therefore,  $P(0,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-2t})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2{e}^{-2t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point  $P(0,1)$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0\,,\,1⟩+u⟨1\,,\,-2⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨et−1,e−2t⟩ at the point P(0,1), valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨1,2⟩
b
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨1,−1⟩
c
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨−1,2⟩
d
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨−1,−2⟩
e
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨1,−2⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The point P(0,1) is at the tip of r(t) for some specific value t0 of the parameter t. At this point, the vector r′(t0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(t0)+ur′(t0),u∈(−∞,∞).

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to P. We know that

r(t)=⟨0,1⟩⟨et−1,e−2t⟩=⟨0,1⟩,

and equating the components yields the following system:

{et−1=0e−2t=1

From the first equation, we get t=0. This value also satisfies the other equation. Therefore, P(0,1) is at the tip of the vector r(0).

We calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(et−1),ddt(e−2t)⟩=⟨et,−2e−2t⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=0:

r′(0)=⟨e0,−2e0⟩=⟨1,−2⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point P(0,1) is
R(u)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨1,−2⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

q-33457.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=({t}^{2}-1)\,i+\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,j+(t-1)\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=2,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
q-33457.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=2$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(2)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r(2)+u{r}^{′}(2),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

First, we find $r(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =({2}^{2}-1)\,i+\sqrt{1+{2}^{2}}\,j+(2-1)\,k \\  & =3\,i+\sqrt{5}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,k \\  & =2t\,i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(2) & =2(2)\,i+\frac{(2)}{\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}}}\,j+\,k \\  & =4\,i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=2$ is 

$$
R(u)=3i+\sqrt{5}\,j+\,k+u(4\,i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=(t2−1)i+1+t2j+(t−1)k at the point corresponding to t=2, valid for all real values of u?

a
3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+k)
b
3i+5j+k+u(5i+15j+k)
c
3i+5j+k+u(5i+25j+2k)
d
3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+2k)
e
3i+5j+k+u(4i+45j+k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=2, the vector r′(2) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(2)+ur′(2),u∈(−∞,∞).

First, we find r(2): r(2)=(22−1)i+1+22j+(2−1)k=3i+5j+k

Now, we calculate r′(t):

r′(t)=ddt(t2−1)i+ddt(1+t2)j+ddt(t−1)k=2ti+t1+t2j+k

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=2:

r′(2)=2(2)i+(2)1+(2)2j+k=4i+25j+k Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=2 is R(u)=3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+k),u∈(−∞,∞).

q-126898.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+2t,4-{t}^{2}⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨0,-1⟩.$
q-126898.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+2,-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨2t+2,-2t⟩ & =0 \\ 0(2t+2)+(-1)(-2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{2}+2(0),4-{0}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,4).$

Question 11
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2+2t,4−t2⟩, find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨0,−1⟩.

a
(3,3) and (0,4)
b
(3,3)
c
(−1,3)
d
(0,4)
e
(1,−4) and (−1,3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(t2+2t),ddt(4−t2)⟩=⟨2t+2,−2t⟩

The vectors ⟨0,−1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if ⟨0,−1⟩⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have ⟨0,−1⟩⋅r′(t)=0⟨0,−1⟩⋅⟨2t+2,−2t⟩=00(2t+2)+(−1)(−2t)=02t=0t=0.

Therefore, the only solution is t=0.

Finally, since r(0)=⟨02+2(0),4−02⟩=⟨0,4⟩, we conclude that ⟨0,−1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (0,4).

q-164846.name: Question 12
q-164846.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=2t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
q-164846.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,j \\  & =2i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [2t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j]\cdot (2i+2t\,j) & =0 \\ 2t\cdot 2+({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 2t & =0 \\ 2t(2+{t}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 2t({t}^{2}+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0$ since ${t}^{2}+1>0$ for any $t.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)=2(0)\,i+((0)^{2}-1)\,j=-j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,-1).$

q-126896.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨1-{t}^{2},3t+4⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1,1⟩.$
q-126896.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-2t,3⟩ & =0 \\ 1(-2t)+1(3) & =0 \\ -2t+3 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=\frac{3}{2}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨1-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2},3(\frac{3}{2})+4⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\frac{9}{4},\frac{9}{2}+4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}).$

The vectors ⟨1,1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if ⟨1,1⟩⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have ⟨1,1⟩⋅r′(t)=0⟨1,1⟩⋅⟨−2t,3⟩=01(−2t)+1(3)=0−2t+3=0t=32.

Therefore, the only solution is t=32.

Finally, since r(32)=⟨1−(32)2,3(32)+4⟩=⟨1−94,92+4⟩=⟨−54,172⟩, we conclude that ⟨1,1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (−54,172).

q-164838.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
q-164838.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j]\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j) & =0 \\ (t+2)\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}} & =0 \\ t+2+t & =0 \\ 2t+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1)=(-1+2)\,i+\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1}\,j=i+\sqrt{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,\sqrt{2}).$

q-165036.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3},3{t}^{2}+4t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,-1⟩.$
q-165036.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,-1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =⟨c,-c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}=c \\ 6t+4=-c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2{t}^{2}.$ Substituting $c=2{t}^{2}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+4 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 2{t}^{2}+6t+4 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}+3t+2 & =0 \\ (t+2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the points corresponding to $t=-2$ and $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3},3(-1)^{2}+4(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{2}{3},-1⟩, \\ r(-2) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-2)^{3},3(-2)^{2}+4(-2)⟩=⟨-\frac{16}{3},4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-\frac{2}{3},-1)$ and $(-\frac{16}{3},4).$

q-32893.name: Question 17
q-32893.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(16+{t}^{3})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
q-32893.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(16+{t}^{3})\,j \\  & =\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ t\,i+(16+{t}^{3})\,j & =c(i+3{t}^{2}\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i,$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}t=c \\ 16+{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}16+{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{3} \\ 16 & =2{t}^{3} \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =2\,i+(16+{2}^{3})\,j \\  & =2\,i+24\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $P(2,24).$

q-126900.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-2t,4t-1⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨-1,1⟩.$
q-126900.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨-1\,,\,1⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨-1,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨-1,1⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,4⟩ & =c⟨-1,1⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,4⟩ & =⟨-c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2t-2=-c \\ 4=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain that $c=4.$ Substituting $c=4$ into the first equation, we get $t=-1.$ 

Therefore, $⟨-1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{2}-2(-1),4(-1)-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-5⟩,\end{aligned}

q-75204.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2t-{t}^{2}\,,\,2{t}^{2}\,,\,2t+{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩.$
q-75204.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩ & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩ & =⟨0\,,\,c\,,\,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2-2t=0 \\ 4t=c \\ 2+2t=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $t=1.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=4.$
These values also satisfy the third equation. 

Therefore, $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2-{1}^{2}\,,\,2\cdot {1}^{2}\,,\,2+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,2,3).$

q-165043.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+(t-1)\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
q-165043.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j \\  & =(2t-2)\,i+\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+(t-1)\,j & =c((2t-2)i+\,j) \\ ({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+(t-1)\,j & =c(2t-2)i+c\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t+2=c(2t-2) \\ t-1=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain $t-1=c.$ Substituting $c=t-1$ into the first equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t+2 & =(t-1)(2t-2) \\ {t}^{2}-2t+2 & =2{t}^{2}-4t+2 \\ {t}^{2}-2t & =0 \\ t(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the points corresponding to $t=0$ and $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =({0}^{2}-2(0)+2)\,i+(0-1)\,j=2\,i-\,j, \\ r(2) & =({2}^{2}-2(2)+2)\,i+(2-1)\,j=2\,i+\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(2,-1)$ and $(2,1).$

Given the curve r(t)=(t2−2t+2)i+(t−1)j, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(2,−1) and (2,1)
b
 (1,0) and (2,1)
c
 (2,−1)
d
 (2,1)
e
 (1,0)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=ddt(t2−2t+2)i+ddt(t−1)j=(2t−2)i+j.

The vectors r′(t) and r(t) are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r(t0)=cr′(t0). So, we have

r(t)=cr′(t)(t2−2t+2)i+(t−1)j=c((2t−2)i+j)(t2−2t+2)i+(t−1)j=c(2t−2)i+cj.

Equating the coefficients of i and j gives:

{t2−2t+2=c(2t−2)t−1=c

From the second equation, we obtain t−1=c. Substituting c=t−1 into the first equality, we get t2−2t+2=(t−1)(2t−2)t2−2t+2=2t2−4t+2t2−2t=0t(t−2)=0.

Therefore, r and r′ are parallel at the points corresponding to t=0 and t=2.

Finally, since r(0)=(02−2(0)+2)i+(0−1)j=2i−j,r(2)=(22−2(2)+2)i+(2−1)j=2i+j, we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are parallel at the points (2,−1) and (2,1).
